theDesign.whyTheConsultIsOutsideTheAppendTransacti: The append re-reads the effective head inside its own immediate transaction (SQLiteEventJournalWriter.appendInTransaction, verified read: `actualRevision = head?.streamRevision ?? 0`, conflict when it differs from input.expectedRevision). A consult that ran in that same transaction could never disagree with it — the optimistic check would compare a value against itself and NO commit could ever conflict, which would make clause two of the task text ('refusals proven against races') vacuous by construction. The consult is therefore a separate read, and the window between it and the append is the race.
theDesign.whyTheBranchStillComesFromInsideTheTrans: The consult returns a revision and nothing else. The branch an append lands on is read inside the prepare arm, as S1 wrote it. An activation committing between the consult and the append therefore cannot be written past: the newly activated candidate's head sits at its base revision (EventHistoryCandidateBuild.seedCandidateJournalHead plants it there), the consulted number does not match, and the append refuses. Carrying a branch id out of the consult would have handed a writer a way onto a superseded branch.
theDesign.whyTheGuardLiftIsConditionedOnTheArmAndN: The mirror does not read the mode. It reads which SOURCE the number came from, which is the property that actually matters: a store-derived number stops describing a journal revision once a tail is superseded (S5's finding), and a head-derived one describes the activated branch by construction. Keying the guard on the arm rather than re-reading the mode keeps one decision in one place and makes the mirror testable without a mode override.
theDesign.identityOrderingPreserved: The consult never refuses. Every refusal still comes from the append, so the journal writer's command-identity check keeps answering BEFORE the head check — a retry that arrives after the stream moved is still reported as a retry, matching DurableMatchStore's own stated ordering rule. Pinned by the surviving duplicate row, which passes a one-revision-stale expectation and gets duplicate-command rather than revision-conflict.

green.raceRealism: Two writers, two SQLite connections to the same campaign file, both consulting the head before either appends. better-sqlite3 runs a transaction synchronously on the one Node thread, so the transactions cannot overlap in time; what IS raced is the consulted view, which is precisely the state a second process would hold. The suite's header says this in as many words and explicitly does not claim a multi-process concurrency harness. The brief recommended the owner accept this framing in the S6 receipt to pre-empt a later 'but is this a REAL race' — this receipt makes that request explicitly.
green.noPartialWriteNoDoubleHead: The loser's event is absent from event_journal_events, the activated branch's head is at 2 (advanced exactly once), and the stream holds exactly two head rows — the live path's and the candidate's — so no second head was minted by the losing append.

rows.SURVIVED_ON_FIRST_RUN: YES, and this is the most important finding of the slice. On the first matrix run M4 survived with 172 suites / 1343 tests ALL GREEN. The reason is a coincidence: on a correctly-rewound stream the candidate's base revision equals the cut, the store's next sequence after supersedeFrom also equals the cut, and journalHeadRevisionForNextMatchSequence is the identity — so head-derived and store-derived produce the SAME number and no rewind fixture can tell them apart. The suite as first written did not pin task 1.6's central claim at all. It was fixed by adding the 'match log has run ahead of it' row: an event appended through store.appendEvent (the shape ServerMatchHost.create leaves, which never crosses the mirror's batch boundary) puts the store's next sequence at 3 while the head is still at 2, and only then do the two sources disagree. riskFlaggedForTheOwner.severity: medium, inert today, load-bearing for S7's ordering
riskFlaggedForTheOwner.text: At mode 'enabled' the consult answers the head's revision UNCONDITIONALLY — including when the match log holds events the journal never received. The batch then lands at the head and the journal's history silently omits those events. This is the create-path gap (ServerMatchHost.create persists opening events through appendEvent, which is not the batch boundary the mirror hooks) seen from the write side, and 'appends at the head when the match log has run ahead of it' asserts it as current behaviour rather than hiding it. The consequence for S7 is an ORDERING constraint: the create-path seeding (R4.S7-a) must land BEFORE the cutover flip, or the first enabled process will build every match's journal history starting from wherever the mirror happened to be, with no record that a prefix is missing. matchAuthorityBaseline already has the vocabulary for the honest version of this ('never invent a prefix'; source 'legacy-baseline' with a firstRetainedRevision) and the write side does not use it. Whether the commit path should instead REFUSE that disagreement is S4-R1's question, which is R4.S7-d's to answer — see s4R1Disposition.

M4 — the mutant that replaces the head's revision with the store's next sequence while keeping the 'journal' label — survived a FULL GREEN gate (172 suites / 1343 tests) on the first matrix run. On a correctly-rewound stream the two sources agree numerically by construction, so no rewind fixture can distinguish them; only a stream where the log has run ahead of the head can. Any later slice that changes the consult should re-run M4 specifically, and any reviewer reading 'the expected revision comes from the journal head' should check that the row proving it is the log-ahead one, not the rewind one.
